::: {.lead}
The *Sunrise* shop has new opening hours from 1 December. Huda, the office
manager, must tell the whole staff at Monday's meeting, and she wants a few
slides on the big screen. Her first try is one slide with seven long
sentences in small black letters. Nobody at the back can read it, and
everybody reads instead of listening. In this lesson you make clear slides
in **PowerPoint**: you choose a **layout**, give the talk one look with a
**theme**, add a **picture** with alt text, and keep **few words** on each
slide. Every section ends with a lab task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary slide-layout placeholder theme designer colour-contrast slide-show >}}

## 17.1 Slides and layouts

PowerPoint opens with a window of three parts: the slide thumbnails on the
left, the big slide in the middle and the notes pane under it
(@fig-window).

![The PowerPoint window and the tabs of today.](images/ppt-window.png){#fig-window width=100%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 17.1 — Layout and placeholder"}
A **layout** is the plan of a slide: where the title, the text and the
pictures go. Each layout has **placeholders**, dashed boxes that say "Click
to add title" or "Click to add text". You click a placeholder and type.
:::

![Four common layouts.](images/layouts.png){#fig-layouts width=100%}

- **Home › New Slide** adds a slide; the arrow under it lets you choose the
  layout.
- **Home › Layout** changes the layout of the slide you are on.
- The first slide uses **Title Slide**; most slides use **Title and
  Content**; **Two Content** puts a list next to a picture.
- **File › Save As** › `shop-hours.pptx`. Press **F5** to start the slide
  show and **Esc** to stop it.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 17.1 — Huda's first two slides"}
1. Slide 1, *Title Slide*: "New shop hours", and under it "Huda, Office
   Manager".
2. Home › New Slide › *Title and Content*: the title "From 1 December" and
   three points in the content placeholder.
3. She saves the file as `shop-hours.pptx`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Drawing your own text boxes on a Blank slide. Then the titles jump from
slide to slide, and the outline and Designer cannot use them. Use the
placeholders of a layout.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/slide-builder.html" poster="sims/slide-builder.png" title="Slide Builder: one good slide" height="820" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Two slides"}
1. Open PowerPoint, choose **Blank Presentation**, and type a title slide
   about a place you know (your title and your name).
2. Add a *Title and Content* slide with three points about the place.
3. Save it as `my-place.pptx`, press F5, and check both slides.

*Your result:* `my-place.pptx` with two slides.
:::

## 17.2 One look for the whole talk: themes and Designer

Huda's slides are black on white. A **theme** gives all of them the same
colours and fonts in one click (@fig-themes).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 17.2 — Theme and Designer"}
A **theme** is a set of colours, fonts and backgrounds for all slides
(**Design** tab). **Designer** (**Design › Designer**, in Microsoft 365)
suggests layouts for the slide you are on; you click one to use it.
:::

![One slide in three themes.](images/themes.png){#fig-themes width=100%}

- **Design** tab › click a theme; the arrow on the right shows more.
- **Variants** (next to the themes) change the colours of the same theme.
- The text must be easy to read: dark text on a light background, or light
  text on a dark background. This is called strong **colour contrast**.
- Designer needs an internet connection; if it is not there, use the
  layouts.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 17.2 — A theme for the hours"}
1. Huda clicks the Design tab and chooses an orange theme like *Sunrise*.
2. Both slides change at once: orange titles, a light background, the same
   font.
3. On slide 2 she opens Designer and picks a design with a clock picture on
   the right.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
A different colour and font on every slide, or light grey text on a light
background. The talk looks messy, and people at the back cannot read it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · A theme"}
1. In `my-place.pptx`, choose a theme on the Design tab, then try two
   Variants.
2. Check the contrast: can you read the text from two metres away?
3. If you have Designer, try two of its ideas on slide 2 and keep one.

*Your result:* `my-place.pptx` with a theme.
:::

## 17.3 Pictures and alt text

A picture helps people remember. It must keep its shape, and it needs
**alt text** for people who cannot see it (@fig-pictures).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 17.3 — Pictures and alt text"}
**Insert › Pictures** adds a picture from your device, from Stock Images or
from the web. **Alt text** is one short sentence that says what the picture
shows; a screen reader reads it aloud for a blind colleague.
:::

![Resize from a corner, and write alt text.](images/pictures.png){#fig-pictures width=100%}

- To resize, drag a **corner** handle: the picture keeps its shape. A side
  handle stretches it.
- Right-click the picture › **View Alt Text** › write one sentence.
- Use your own photos, Stock Images, or pictures you are allowed to use;
  not any picture from the web.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 17.3 — The photo of the shop"}
1. On slide 2, Huda clicks Insert › Pictures › This Device and chooses her
   photo of the shop.
2. She drags a corner to make it smaller, and moves it to the right.
3. Alt text: "The Sunrise shop next to the bus stop."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Making a picture fit by dragging a side handle. The shop becomes tall and
thin, and people laugh at the picture instead of listening.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · A picture"}
1. Add a third slide with the layout *Two Content*: three points on the
   left, a picture of your place on the right (your photo or Stock Images).
2. Resize it from a corner and write its alt text.

*Your result:* `my-place.pptx` with three slides and a picture with alt
text.
:::

## 17.4 Few words on each slide

The slide helps the speaker; it does not replace the speaker
(@fig-text).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 17.4 — The few-words rule"}
Each slide has **one idea**, a short title and **3 to 5 points**, each of a
few words (about 8 or fewer). The details are what you **say**. The text
is big enough to read from the back: about 24 pt or more.
:::

![Seven sentences or four short points.](images/text-amount.png){#fig-text width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 17.4 — From seven sentences to four points"}
1. Huda's first slide has seven long sentences.
2. She keeps four points: "Sun–Thu: 9:00–20:00", "Friday: closed",
   "Saturday: 10:00–18:00", "From 1 December".
3. "Tell every customer" and "Rana puts a notice on the door" are things she
   says, not things on the slide.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Making the font smaller so that all sentences fit. The problem is too much
text, not a too big font.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Fewer words"}
1. Check every slide of `my-place.pptx`: at most five points, and each point
   at most eight words.
2. Move the long details into the **notes pane** under the slide.
3. Press F5 and look at the slides as the audience.

*Your result:* `my-place.pptx`, three clear slides.
:::

## Case study: Slide Doctor

Huda's colleagues send her slides for the Monday meeting, and each slide has
one problem: seven long sentences, light grey text on light blue, a photo of
the shop that is too tall and thin, a photo without alt text, and a
"Thank you!" slide in the wrong layout. The Game challenge of the
interactive lesson uses these slides. In the mini-game below you choose the
best fix for each one.

{{< sim file="sims/slide-doctor.html" poster="sims/slide-doctor.png" title="Slide Doctor: fix the slide" kind="game" height="620" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Huda's talk"}
1. Make Huda's talk in a new file `shop-hours.pptx`: a title slide, a slide
   with the new hours, a slide "Why the change?" with two points, and a
   "Thank you! Questions?" slide in a title layout.
2. Use one theme, few words, and one picture with alt text.
3. Upload `my-place.pptx` and `shop-hours.pptx` to the e-learning platform.

*Your result:* `shop-hours.pptx` with four clear slides.
:::

## Exercises

1. What is a layout?
2. What is a placeholder?
3. Which layout fits the first slide of a talk?
4. Where do you choose a theme?
5. What does Designer do?
6. Why is light grey text on a light background a problem?
7. How do you resize a picture without stretching it?
8. What is alt text, and who needs it?
9. How many points should a slide have?
10. Where do the details go that are not on the slide?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. The plan of a slide: where the title, the text and the pictures go.
2. A dashed box of a layout where you click and type or add a picture.
3. Title Slide.
4. On the Design tab.
5. It suggests designs for the slide you are on.
6. The contrast is weak: people at the back cannot read it.
7. Drag a corner handle, not a side handle.
8. One sentence that says what the picture shows; a screen reader reads it
   for people who cannot see the picture.
9. About 3 to 5 short points.
10. In what the speaker says (and in the notes pane).
:::
